This app’s name is an homage to the world’s first web server. Back in 1989, Tim Berners-Lee started the web on his NeXT computer.

On that computer was an app named WorldWideWeb. This app was unique because it allowed his machine to edit and serve HTML documents. The app also used coding frameworks that were adopted by Apple after purchasing NeXT: they are being used right now to display what you’re reading.

WebProxyTool allows you to capture and display all of the data that is sent and received by other apps on your device. 

How it works:
The app creates local on-device server and directs all outgoing HTTPS traffic to it. App provides locally generated trust certificate which should be installed and trusted by user to decrypt HTTPS traffic. When it is done app captures HTTPS requests, makes dummy leaf certificates for requested domains and acts as man-in-the-middle proxy to read and store data. Data is stored only in local device database and WebProxyTool developers do not have access to it. The app works without any remote servers involved.
